newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking French truckers block ports, German border.
newsitem.headline: Striking French truckers block ports, German border.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers blocked Channel ports and German border crossings on Monday, stepping up economic pressure on the government on the eighth day of the most serious labour unrest in France this year.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe renewed a pressing appeal to truckers and haulage companies to reach a deal after all-night talks with a government mediator failed to break the deadlock.
The strikers, whose roadblocks around the nation are squeezing the economy, demand higher wages, shorter hours and retirement at age 55 rather than 60.

"I'm following the talks hour by hour," conservative Juppe said in the south-western city of Bordeaux. "The government has done everything to get these talks under way. They must now resume and finish".
After their abortive 14-hour session, unions and bosses agreed to meet for a new round on Monday hosted by mediator Robert Cros at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT) at the Transport Ministry.
The dispute is the most serious wave of unrest since a 24-day round of public sector strikes against the centre-right government almost paralysed the country in late 1995.

The truckers, buoyed by an opinion poll showing broad public support, hardened their protests around the country, blocking the Channel ports of Calais and Boulogne as well as five frontier crossings with Germany in Alsace.
They let cars and buses embark on Channel ferries and cross into Germany, but stopped trucks including at frontier crossings at Strasbourg, Gambsheim, Beinheim, Lauterbourg and Wissembourg.
The action added to the woes of cross-Channel travellers, already hit by the closure of the Channel Tunnel to all but freight trains after a fire last week.

Some 300 trucks arriving from Britain were blocked at Calais with dozens of others blocked going the other way. Other drivers wanting to cross to Britain sought to drive to the Belgian ports of Zeebrugge or Antwerp.

The road information centre said there were 98 truckers' barricades on major routes in France on Monday morning, up from 62 on Sunday night, with tens of thousands of trucks involved, not mentioning disruption to smaller routes.

Truckers targeted oil refineries and fuel depots, blocking industrial zones in Le Havre and Rouen in the north-west, and cutting off the last petrol depot still accessible in the Pyrenees-Atlantiques region, at Boucau near Bayonne.
In the south-western city of Bordeaux, most petrol stations had run out of supplies. Bordeaux has been singled out for one of the tightest nooses because Juppe is mayor of the city.

The protests also crept closer to Paris. Access roads to the Rungis wholesale food market were blocked and the main motorway north of the capital was cut to one lane on the southbound carriage near Roissy airport.
An IPSOS opinion poll for France-2 television showed an overwhelming 74 percent of French people sympathised with the strikers and 87 percent found their demands "rather justified".

The companies have agreed to allow truckers to retire at 55 instead of 60, but want the state to foot the bill. The opposition Socialist Party urged the government to put pressure on haulage companies to settle the dispute.

The Force Ouvriere union urged members in other transport sectors -- air, rail, ships and buses -- to "express sympathy with the truck drivers". It did not spell out whether this could mean disrupting traffic.
